children: Nvidia's revenue growth and $130 billion quarterly forecast showed that demand for chips is still sky-high
Nvidia CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress hinted at a more disciplined approach to financing players in the AI ecosystem.
After a blowout quarter, Nvidia expressed confidence in the demand trajectory ahead as it plans to move forward without co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang.

That was the takeaway from the company's October-quarter earnings results and call on Tuesday, which sent its stock (NVDA) up 3.8% in after-hours trading. Granted, it will take more than that to reverse the recent pressure on Nvidia shares, which closed Tuesday at $155.46, down over 36% from their October highs. They've traded 10.5% lower since Huang stepped down last week.
Nvidia's latest quarterly results topped expectations, with data-center revenue more than doubling from a year earlier, in a sign that the artificial-intelligence buildout remains in full swing.
The company also issued a forecast for $130 billion in revenue during the January quarter, above Wall Street estimates for $125 billion.

The $130 billion projection "was the most important line in the release," Yorkville Ives analyst Daniel Ives said. On the call, Nvidia CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress also raised the company's forecast for its next fiscal year, which now calls for 75% revenue growth, up from a 70% projection previously.
Pushing back against recent whispers of Huang potentially returning to Nvidia, Chairman Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that the company does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.

"The tone of the call sent the message that Nvidia is moving forward without Jensen Huang without saying so explicitly," Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said in emailed comments. In his view, "Kress led that message, projecting optimism, confidence and a clear sense of direction for the company's future."

To Tejas Dessai, the director of thematic research at ETF provider Global X, the earnings "offer a powerful counternarrative to the recent AI selloff" and show that "AI doesn't have a demand problem."
On the earnings call, Kress affirmed the strength of Nvidia's offerings in the face of increased competition from companies designing their own chips.

Nvidia expects adjusted gross margins, or the amount of money it brings in after accounting for the cost of goods sold, to be between 71% and 72% next quarter, down from 74.9% in the October quarter. The margin compression isn't a sign that Nvidia's pricing power is eroding, though, according to management.

Kress said margins temporarily dipped as a result of Nvidia honoring the pricing on existing customer orders. She added that margins should bottom in the January quarter and rebound throughout next fiscal year as the company reprices its products.

Kress also reaffirmed the company's commitment to supporting the overall AI ecosystem. However, she struck a more cautious tone, sharing that Nvidia will be "disciplined and selective" with future investments. The company will favor physical "land, power and shell" bottlenecks, while encouraging its investment-grade customers to use their balance sheets to support the buildout, Kress said.
The commentary was enough to give shares of neoclouds a boost. Shares of CoreWeave (CRWV), Nebius (NBIS) and Iren (IREN) all rose more than 9% in Tuesday's extended session.
